paper_metadata.title: Temperature effects on low cycle fatigue deformation of powder metallurgy superalloy FGH95

evidence.quote: The macroscopic morphology and microstructure evolution mechanism of the FGH95 alloy were investigated with regard to fracture under low-cycle fatigue at different temperatures.

Tests were conducted at temperatures of 420 ◦ C (T420), 510 ◦ C (T510), and 600 ◦ C (T600).

initially, a solution treatment at 1140 ◦ C for 3.5 h
subsequently, a salt bath treatment at 650 ◦ C for 15 min, followed by cooling in air to room temperature
The aging treatment involved processing at 874 ◦ C for 1 h, followed by treatment at 650 ◦ C for 24 h.
the specimen surfaces were polished to a mirror finish
the phase structure of the FGH95 specimens remains face- centered cubic (FCC) following LCF tests at T420, T510, and T600
The precipitated phase was identified through selected area diffraction (SAED) and was found to be γ’ phase.
dislocations assume the form of dislocation II, which bypasses the γ’ precipitated phase for motion and deformation.
the FGH95 alloy comprises a matrix phase framework comprising Co and Cr elements and a precipitated structure comprising Ni, Al, and Ti elements
At higher temperatures (T600), dislocations slip on the slip surface of the matrix phase and climb through the phase boundary between the two phases.
elemental analysis revealed the presence of unmelted Zr within the alloy, which is a consequence of the powder metallurgical process

At T420, the dislocation structure of the FGH95 alloy is comprised primarily of two distinct types of dislocations: dislocation I and dislocation II ( Fig. 9 (a) ). Dislocation I is predominantly a shear γ’ precipitation phase
a small quantity of dislocation II is wrapped around the γ’ precipitation phase to form a dislocation ring-like structure
At T600, the dislocation structure within the alloy is primarily represented by dislocation II, which forms a dislocation ring structure surrounding the γ’ precipitated phase

At low temperatures, both the γ matrix phase and the γ’ precipitated phase possess the capacity to resist shear stress and positive stress. Furthermore, the two phases are capable of undergoing shear deformation in response to the shear stress component.
The dislocation structure primarily traverses the matrix phase via bypassing the γ’ precipitated phase.
dislocations assume the form of dislocation II, which bypasses the γ’ precipitated phase for motion and deformation.

evidence.section: 3.3. Fatigue crack initiation and fracture mode
evidence.quote: At high temperatures, the strength of the matrix phase structure decreases, while the strength of the precipitation phase increases. It can be reasonably postulated that the change in temperature is related to the transformation in fracture form and precipitate structure.
At low temperatures (T420 and T510), dislocations primarily move along the slip surface, resulting in crack initiation along the slip zone.
At higher temperatures (T600), dislocations slip on the slip surface of the matrix phase and climb through the phase boundary between the two phases

conflicts.description: The fracture temperature at the second shear-fracture condition is reported inconsistently as 510 °C in the Abstract and 550 °C in Section 3.2.
